prize_parts.citation: For the development of palladium-catalysed carbon-nitrogen cross-coupling, a general method for constructing arylamines

statement.case_for: Buchwald-Hartwig amination is the clearest case on the shortlist of a new chemical reaction that became routine. Before the mid-1990s aryl C-N bond formation relied on harsh, substrate-limited methods (SNAr, Ullmann-type chemistry). Ligand design, bulky biaryl phosphines and chelating bisphosphines, backed by mechanistic work on oxidative addition, amine binding and reductive elimination, made it broad and predictable. Three decades on it is among the most-used reactions in medicinal and process chemistry and in materials, and its adoption is visible in an enormous number of later syntheses. Five of eight members ranked it, and every member who proposed laureates named Buchwald and Hartwig, so attribution is as clean as it gets in this field. It is core molecule-making chemistry, with no border-field question about what was new chemically.
statement.case_against: The 2010 prize already honoured palladium cross-coupling, and some colleagues may see C-N coupling as an extension of that logic. Kosugi's earlier tin-amide coupling is a genuine precursor, so priority has to be stated carefully in the citation. The method is also less novel as a concept than targeted protein degradation or massively parallel sequencing, and it has less visible reach beyond chemistry. It has only one first-place vote and middling support, so it may not win a majority against the more broadly consequential candidates.

responses.point: Linke ranked B035 eighth, noting that the 2010 cross-coupling prize may make the committee reluctant to honour another coupling advance, though he accepts its mechanistic clarity and industrial maturity.
responses.response: I take the 2010 overlap seriously but disagree on its weight. That prize rewarded C-C bond formation with organometallic partners (Heck, Negishi, Suzuki). C-N coupling needed different ligand architecture and a different rate-limiting step, reductive elimination from an amido complex, which is why it came only two decades later. Chemists use it as a separate tool, not as a variant of Suzuki. The Nobel record has repeatedly recognised distinct advances inside one field, for example metathesis and asymmetric catalysis. I would still accept that this concern might sink B035 if the committee wants breadth across sub-fields.

responses.point: Aqvist put B011 (massively parallel sequencing) first as the clearest game-changer, a chemical solution with overdue recognition, and also ranked B035 fourth as simple, general and industrially routine.
responses.response: I agree that sequencing has had the largest downstream effect on science, and I rank it high. My reservation is attribution: the credited names (Balasubramanian, Klenerman, Rothberg, Ju, Mayer) do not map to one clean discovery, and the technology was built by companies and large teams. That makes a three-person citation hard to defend and risks the prize reading as a technology award. The Buchwald-Hartwig attribution has no such problem. I would back B011 if we can agree on a defensible trio, but I do not think its impact alone outweighs a clear attribution advantage.

responses.point: Aili ranked B010 (targeted protein degradation) first for turning induced proximity into a design principle, proposing Crews, Deshaies and Handa, and notes that clinical approval is not yet established.
responses.response: As a synthetic chemist I find the PROTAC concept elegant, and the cereblon story explains thalidomide-class drugs. My questions are what was new chemically and whether it is mature. The key advance is a biological mechanism hijacked with a heterobifunctional molecule, closer to chemical biology and pharmacology than to a new reaction. With no approved PROTAC yet, there is a risk of recognising a modality before it has delivered. The attribution is also unsettled: Ciulli, Gray and Sakamoto made decisive contributions, and three names will exclude real credit. I could support B010 later, but not ahead of B035 now.

responses.point: Sparr ranked B035 fourth and B046 (phase separation) first, noting that the Buchwald-Hartwig method is transformative in pharmaceutical and materials chemistry even though synthesis is outside her field.
responses.response: I appreciate the support for B035 and your point that two laureates is a natural attribution. On phase separation, the concept is important, but I am not convinced yet. Several members, including Linke, acknowledge the active debate on which cellular condensates are truly phase-separated, and the chemistry is largely polymer physics applied to biology. I would want that debate to settle before honouring it. I would be interested in how you rate the Hyman, Brangwynne and Rosen attribution against Pappu's and Mittag's sequence-grammar contributions.

uncertainties: Whether the committee will treat C-N coupling as a distinct achievement from the 2010 cross-coupling prize or as an extension of it.
How to word the citation so that Kosugi's earlier tin-amide precedent is not misrepresented while still limiting the prize to Buchwald and Hartwig.
Whether a prize rooted in synthetic methodology can gain a majority against B010, B011 and B046, which have more first-place support and wider reach.
Whether B010 will be mature enough in clinical terms for me to move it up in later rounds.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from the provided profile. I trained with Masamune at MIT and have no known personal or institutional ties to Buchwald, Hartwig or Kosugi. I share a university with Heiner Linke and Emma Sparr, but none of the shortlisted candidates is from Lund.
